'''''Phaseolus coccineus''''', known as '''runner bean''',<ref name=GRIN>{{GRIN | access-date = 16 December 2017}}</ref> '''scarlet runner bean''',<ref name=GRIN /> or '''multiflora bean''',<ref name=GRIN /> is a plant in the legume family, [[Fabaceae]]. Another common name is '''butter bean''',<ref>{{cite book |title=Cereals and Pulses |editor=M. Brink |editor2=G. Belay |publisher=[[Plant Resources of Tropical Africa|PROTA]] |year=2006 |isbn=90-5782-170-2 |volume=Plant Resources of Tropical Africa 1 |page=139}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=''Phaseolus coccineus L.'' |url=https://webapps2.cfans.umn.edu/herbarium/Detail.aspx?SpCode=452 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170927111813/https://webapps2.cfans.umn.edu/herbarium/Detail.aspx?SpCode=452 |url-status=dead |archive-date=September 27, 2017 |work=Strand Memorial Herbarium |publisher=[[University of Minnesota]] |date=2016 |access-date=September 27, 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Phaseolus coccineus (runner bean) |url=http://www.cabi.org/isc/datasheet/40618 |publisher=[[CABI (organisation)|CABI]] |journal=Invasive Species Compendium |date=2019 |doi=10.1079/cabicompendium.40618 |access-date=September 26, 2017|url-access=subscription }}</ref> which can also refer to the [[lima bean]], a different species.

It is grown both as a food plant and an [[ornamental plant]].

== Description ==
[[File:Scarlet Runner beans.jpg|thumb|Beans of 'Scarlet Runner' cultivar. A similar cultivar, the Japanese runner, looks the same but is almost twice as large.<ref>{{cite web |last1=No Coast Seeds |title=Bean - Shinshu Runner |url=https://nocoastseeds.ca/products/bean-shinshu-runner |website=nocoastseeds.ca |access-date=16 April 2023}} The website shows a side-by-side picture of the Scarlet runner and the Japanese runner.</ref>]]
This species originated in the mountains of [[Central America]]. It was most likely cultivated in the highlands of Mexico and Guatemala around 2000 BC.<ref>{{cite book |editor1-last=Prance |editor1-first=Ghillean |editor2-last=Nesbitt |editor2-first=Mark |last1=Pearman |first1=Georgina |date=2005 |title=The Cultural History of Plants |publisher=Routledge |page=146 |isbn=0415927463}}</ref> Most varieties have red [[flower]]s and multicolored [[seeds]] (though some have white flowers and white seeds) and are often grown as [[ornamental plant]]s. The vine can grow to {{convert|3|m|ft}} or more in length,<ref>{{cite AV media|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=u4BOysBQrs0|title=Scarlet Runner Beans – GROWS 10' TALL!! Ancient Beans for Cool Weather|date=18 August 2012|work=YouTube}}</ref> its pods can get to  {{convert|25|cm|inch}}, and its beans about {{convert|2.5|cm|inch}} long.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.gardenia.net/plant/phaseolus-coccineus|title=Phaseolus coccineus - Runner Beans|accessdate=2023-11-18}}www.gardenia.net</ref>

It differs from the [[common bean]] (''P. vulgaris'') in several respects: the [[cotyledon]]s stay in the ground during [[germination]], and the plant is a [[Perennial plant|perennial]] [[vine]] with tuberous [[root]]s (though it is frequently treated as an annual in colder climates).{{cn|date=June 2024}}

The knife-shaped pods are normally green; however, there are rare varieties bred by amateurs that have purple pods. An example of such a purple-podded runner bean is 'Aeron Purple Star'.<ref name="APS">{{cite web |url = http://www.aeronvale-allotments.org.uk/aeronpurplestar|title = Aeron Purple Star Runner Bean Seeds|access-date = 2014-09-13}}</ref>

Runner beans have also been called "Oregon lima bean",<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.beeculture.com/content/pollination_handbook/scarlet.html|title=The Beekeeping Resource Leader – Bee Culture Magazine|work=Bee Culture|access-date=2010-08-16|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110707222532/http://www.beeculture.com/content/pollination_handbook/scarlet.html|archive-date=2011-07-07|url-status=dead}}</ref> and in [[Nahuatl]] {{lang|nah|ayocotl}} or in Spanish {{lang|es|ayocote}}. Runner beans, like all [[bean]]s, contain the [[toxic]] [[protein]] [[phytohaemagglutinin]] and thus should be cooked well before eating.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://davesgarden.com/guides/articles/view/2385/|title=Beans! Beans! The Poisonous Fruit! - Dave's Garden|website=davesgarden.com|access-date=2018-07-24}}</ref>

== Uses ==

Runner beans were grown as food plants in North America and Europe from the 1600s, and also as ornamentals for their attractive flowers. However, they came to be used primarily as a garden ornamental plant in North America, including for temporary screening. The flowers attract [[hummingbirds]], bees and other insects. In the UK and other European countries – where the vegetable is a popular choice for kitchen gardens and allotments – the flowers came to be ignored, or treated as an attractive bonus to cultivating the plant for the beans.<ref name="UWisconsin">{{cite web |last1=Mahr |first1=Susan |title=Scarlet Runner Bean, Phaseolus coccineus |url=https://hort.extension.wisc.edu/articles/scarlet-runner-bean-phaseolus-coccineus/ |website=Wisconsin Horticulture |publisher=University of Wisconsin - Madison |access-date=16 November 2022}}</ref><ref name="Kew">{{cite web |last1=Dove |first1=Helena |last2=McHale |first2=Ellen |title=Bountiful beans |url=https://www.kew.org/read-and-watch/runner-beans-kitchen-garden |website=Royal Botanic Garden Kew |access-date=16 November 2022}}</ref>

It is a plant visited by [[Honey bee|honeybees]] for both [[pollen]] and [[nectar]], from which they produce a monofloral honey that is traditionally appreciated in [[Poland]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kot |first=Izabela |last2=Lisecka |first2=Magdalena |last3=Kmieć |first3=Katarzyna |last4=Golan |first4=Katarzyna |last5=Górska-Drabik |first5=Edyta |last6=Kiljanek |first6=Tomasz |last7=Zimowska |first7=Beata |last8=Skwaryło-Bednarz |first8=Barbara |date=2023-11-13 |title=Visitation of Apis mellifera L. in Runner Bean (Phaseolus coccineus L.) and Its Exposure to Seasonal Agrochemicals in Agroecosystems |url=https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0472/13/11/2138 |journal=Agriculture |language=en |volume=13 |issue=11 |pages=2138 |doi=10.3390/agriculture13112138  |doi-access=free|issn=2077-0472 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240619140617/https://www.mdpi.com/2077-0472/13/11/2138 |archive-date=2024-06-19}}</ref>

The seeds of the plant can be used fresh or as dried beans. The pods are eaten whole while young and not yet fibrous, though they tend to have a rougher surface than the [[common bean]]. The starchy roots of this perennial are eaten in [[Mesoamerica]].<ref name="UWisconsin" />

The beans are used in many cuisines. It is a popular side vegetable in British cuisine. A variety named 'Judión de la Granja' producing large, white, edible beans is cultivated in [[San Ildefonso]], Spain.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://eng.judionesdelagranja.com/2008/09/07/judiones/|title=Judiones|date=7 September 2008|access-date=8 November 2008|work=Judiones de la Granja|archive-date=29 June 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160629044353/http://eng.judionesdelagranja.com/2008/09/07/judiones/|url-status=dead}}</ref> It is the basis of a [[Province of Segovia|Segovian]] regional dish also named ''Judiones de la Granja'', in which the beans are mixed with [[pig's ear (food)|pig's ears]], [[pig's trotters]], and [[chorizo]], amongst other ingredients.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://eng.judionesdelagranja.com/2008/06/22/judiones-de-la-granja-recipe/|title=Judiones de La Granja recipe|date=22 June 2008|access-date=8 November 2008|work=Judiones de la Granja}}</ref>

In Greece, cultivars of the runner bean with white blossom and white beans are known as ''fasolia gigantes'' (φασόλια γίγαντες). They are grown under protective law in the north of Greece within the regions of [[Kato Nevrokopi]], [[Florina]] and [[Kastoria]].<ref name="EC">{{cite web|url=http://ec.europa.eu/agriculture/quality/door/list.html?recordStart=0&recordPerPage=10&recordEnd=10&sort.milestone=desc&filter.dossierNumber=&filter.comboName=gigantes&filterMin.milestone__mask=&filterMin.milestone=&filterMax.milestone__mask=&filterMax.milestone=&filter.country=&filter.category=&filter.type=&filter.status=REGISTERED|title=DOOR|work=europa.eu |date=24 October 2023 }}</ref> The beans have an important role in Greek cuisine, appearing in many dishes (such as [[Gigantes plaki]]). In English, they are sometimes colloquially referred to as elephant beans.<ref>{{Cite news|url=http://www.menshealth.com/recipes/greek-elephant-beans|title=Greek Elephant Beans|date=2016-03-31|newspaper=Men's Health|access-date=2016-12-26}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.thestar.com/life/food_wine/recipes/2010/03/03/baked_elephant_beans.html|title=Baked elephant beans {{!}} Toronto Star|newspaper=The Toronto Star|date=3 March 2010|access-date=2016-12-26}}</ref> In Austria the coloured versions are cultivated and served as "Käferbohnen" ("beetle-bean"), a dish made of the dry beans with [[pumpkin seed oil]]. It is considered a typical dish of regional Austrian cuisine, but dried runner beans are also consumed to a small extent in Germany. In Turkey, runner beans are the main ingredient in bean [[Pilaki]] and [[Piyaz]].{{cn|date=June 2024}}

Greece and northern Africa are the sources of pods of the runner beans sold as "green beans" in European markets during the cold period. The pods can be identified by their flatness, big size and the rougher surface.

* 'Black Runner'

* 'Case Knife'

Vines bear red flowers and flat, thick and curved pods".</ref> or "Shinshu runner"<ref>{{cite web |last1=No Coast Seeds |title=Bean - Shinshu Runner |url=https://nocoastseeds.ca/products/bean-shinshu-runner |website=nocoastseeds.ca |access-date=16 April 2023}}</ref>
* 'Painted Lady'

''P. coccineus'' subsp. ''darwinianus '' is a cultivated subspecies, commonly referred to as the ''botil'' bean in Mexico.

The related species considered most useful for interbreeding with ''P. coccineus'' to increase its genetic diversity are [[Phaseolus dumosus|''P. dumosus'']] and ''[[Phaseolus vulgaris|P. vulgaris]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.cwrdiversity.org/checklist/genepool-details.php?id%5b%5d=35|title=The Harlan and de Wet Crop Wild Relative Inventory – chapter: ''Phaseolus coccineus''|access-date=12 Sep 2013|publisher=Global Crop Diversity Trust, the Millennium Seed Bank of the Royal Botanic Gardens Kew, and the Government of Norway}}{{Dead link|date=November 2024 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>
